blocks.content: Docker caches every layer it builds, and reuses that cache automatically whenever it can. Understanding exactly when the cache is reused, and when it is thrown away, is one of the highest-leverage things you can learn for fast builds.
1. A Cache Hit Skips Rebuilding a Layer Entirely
blocks.text: 1. A Cache Hit Skips Rebuilding a Layer Entirely

blocks.content: When Docker builds an image, it checks each instruction against its cache: if that exact instruction, in that exact position, with the same input, was already built before, Docker reuses the existing layer instead of running the instruction again.

blocks.alt: An unchanged instruction is simply reused, not rebuilt

blocks.content: 2. One Change Invalidates Everything After It
blocks.text: 2. One Change Invalidates Everything After It

blocks.content: The cache is strictly sequential: the moment one instruction's cache is invalidated (because the instruction itself or its input changed), every single layer after it in the Dockerfile is rebuilt too, even if those later instructions themselves did not change at all.

blocks.alt: A single break in the chain rebuilds everything downstream

blocks.content: 3. Instruction Order Is a Real Performance Decision
blocks.text: 3. Instruction Order Is a Real Performance Decision

blocks.content: This cascading invalidation is exactly why Dockerfiles are written to put rarely-changing steps first. Copying just a dependency manifest and installing dependencies before copying the rest of your application code means that changing application code, which happens constantly, does not force a dependency reinstall on every single build.

blocks.alt: Stable steps first, volatile steps last

blocks.content:
# Good ordering: dependency install survives code-only changes
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .

# Bad ordering: any code change forces a full reinstall
COPY . .
RUN npm install

blocks.content: A well-ordered Dockerfile with a warm cache can turn a multi-minute build into a build that finishes in seconds, since only the last, small layer (usually the app code copy) actually needs to run again.

blocks.alt: The right ordering is the difference between minutes and seconds

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Docker's build cache works layer by layer, and one invalidated layer forces every layer after it to rebuild too.
Ordering a Dockerfile from least-volatile to most-volatile instructions is the single biggest lever for fast, cache-friendly builds.
